rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
rows.description: The person compares their inside doubts with colleagues' outside confidence and stays silent in meetings. Silence then makes them less visible, which feeds the belief they add little.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.
A child faces a test, a dog or a new class, and the stomach knots and the heart thumps. The body's alarm feels like proof that something is truly dangerous.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
A schoolchild says ugh at a chore or a smelly item and aha at a discovery. Ugh signals disgust, boredom or mild annoyance; aha marks a sudden click of understanding that a teacher can celebrate.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A quiet, satisfied chortle can mean genuine amusement, smug pleasure or relief. Context decides: shared humour bonds people, but the same sound aimed at someone's mistake can feel mocking.
